newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa sees decision on sugar beet mill in April.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa sees decision on sugar beet mill in April.

text.p: A decision to go ahead with South Africa's first sugar beet mill, which could produce around 80,000 tonnes of sugar in the Eastern Cape province, is expected to be taken this month, an industry official said on Wednesday.
The project is planned for a site near King Williams' Town on the Fish River and was initiated by the East Cape Agricultural Co-operative.
Co-op chief executive George Ward told Reuters, "We hope a decision will be made in April."
He said German agricultural consultants were putting the final touches to a feasibility study while a group of German investors -- whom he declined to name -- had expressed interest.
"It couldn't start before 1998. Probably 18 months from when the button is pressed," Ward said.
Ward said a mothballed sugar beet mill -- with a capacity of 4,000 tonnes a day -- would be imported from the former East Germany and set up in South Africa as part of the project.
"We are just moving the whole plant out," Ward said.
The sugar beet mill would be erected at a cost of between 260 million to 300 million rand.
Ward said the Eastern Cape region had the ideal climate for growing sugar beet -- which would first be grown in a 150 km radius around the planned mill.
Initial results had shown a yield of around 60 tonnes of beet a hectare with a sucrose content of 16.8/17 percent, Ward said.
The growing season would be five months.
In addition to the sugar produced, the plant could produce around 32,000 tonnes of feed for diary farmers, Ward said.
South Africa's domestic and export requirements are currently filled from sugar cane grown mainly in the KwaZulu-Natal sugarbelt and parts of Mpumulanga province.
Industry officials said last year there were no immediate plans for expanding sugar cane growing areas.
South Africa expected 1996/97 sugar output of 2.27 million tonnes -- the best in several years.
The industry produced only 1.67 million tonnes in the 1995/96 season and was just emerging from five years of drought that the industry said cost it millions of rand in lost revenue.
